transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-09-18
Start: 15:30 UTC
Duration: ~62 minutes
Attendees: Alyssa Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Ramos (Redwood SE), Priya Nair (Nimbus Head of ML), Ben Turner (Nimbus Infra), Samir Patel (Nimbus CTO)

Auto-summary (auto-generated): Discussed continuous batching knobs and expected throughput improvements; agreed to run dedicated pilot. Some transcription artifacts present.

[00:00] Alyssa Chen: hey everyone, thanks for joining. just to set context, today's deep dive is on throughput tuning — continuous batching, scheduler knobs like max_num_seqs, batch timeouts, token limits, kv cache effects, and quantization. diego and i will drive the technical parts.
[00:12] Priya Nair: thanks, alyssa. goal from our side is 3k concurrent qps at 95%ile latency < 200ms on average prompt lengths ~120 tokens. we have bursty traffic so want predictable tail behavior.
[00:25] Diego Ramos: cool. quick clarifier — is that 3k concurrent requests or 3k sequences per second? there's a slight diff in how we count sequences vs requests when batching.
[00:32] Priya Nair: good point — 3k requests/s, typical request is single sequence, but some multi-turn sessions will send prefix+query. around 8% of requests are multi-seq.
[00:42] Ben Turner: infra note — we're planning dedicated capacity on AWS p4d initially, but we may do on-prem later. network egress and cross-az latency matter.
[00:50] Diego Ramos: perfect. so we'll talk about the scheduler topology. Redwood's continuous batching uses a windowed micro-batcher that accumulates seqs up to either max_num_seqs or max_batch_tokens or until batch_timeout_ms fires. default knobs bias for latency, but you can shift them for throughput.
[01:12] Samir Patel: when you say max_num_seqs, is that per-GPU or per-inference worker?
[01:16] Diego Ramos: per-worker deck — the runtime has a pool of inference workers (one per model replica/stream). each worker assembles requests into an attention batch. so max_num_seqs of 64 means that worker will pack up to 64 sequences before dispatching.
[01:28] Alyssa Chen: and important nuance — if you raise max_num_seqs, you get better GPU utilization and higher throughput but risk higher single-request latency for the first seq in the batch. there's also token limits — max_batch_tokens can constrain long sequences.
[01:41] Priya Nair: we have variable seq lengths; 95th perc tokens ~220. will max_batch_tokens then prevent some long requests from joining the main batch?
[01:49] Diego Ramos: yes, long sequences can be isolated into their own micro-batches. we have heuristics to avoid head-of-line blocking — very long sequences often get sent immediately to avoid stalling the queue. but that reduces packing efficiency.
[02:02] Ben Turner: what's the guidance on batch_timeout_ms? we get very spiky traffic, with idle periods then big spikes.
[02:08] Diego Ramos: batch_timeout_ms is your safety net. lower = lower latency, higher = higher throughput. For p4d and your target, we often set batch_timeout_ms between 5-20ms when aiming for sub-200ms 95th. If you want max throughput at expense of latency, 30-50ms can help. but careful with SLAs.
[02:26] Priya Nair: can we do adaptive timeouts? like increase timeout during known off-peak windows?
[02:31] Diego Ramos: yes — Redwood supports autoscaling policies with dynamic scheduler hints. you can feed traffic metrics into the routing layer; our recommendation is dynamic timeouts per-route. we can show a config snippet. (link: ./configs/scheduler_hints.md)
[02:44] Samir Patel: kv cache — how does prefix caching interact with batching? if we have long conversations and many repeated prefixes, does that reduce token compute a lot?
[02:52] Diego Ramos: good question. KV cache reduces repeated prefix decoding cost by keeping the transformer key/value states. From batching perspective, cached prefixes shorten decode time per request, but they also change batching behavior because cached requests may still need to be synchronized at the decode step. in practice we see 20-40% token cost reduction for heavy prefix reuse. but cache warmup matters.
[03:10] Priya Nair: what's the warmup time like? our dataset has lots of short-lived sessions — will caching still help?
[03:14] Diego Ramos: if sessions are short-lived, cache hit rate drops. for many short sessions, continuous batching plus micro-caching (per-request prefix) can still help a bit; but the biggest wins are for long-lived chat sessions or many reuses of the same system prompt.
[03:25] Ben Turner: any pitfalls for VPC/on-prem? we will likely do VPC first then on-prem for data residency.
[03:31] Diego Ramos: two things: network latency between control plane and private endpoints, and available GPU kernel optimizations depending on OS/drivers. on-prem setups sometimes need a one-off kernel/driver tuning for optimal throughput. and watch egress — keep the GPUs in the same subnet to avoid cross-az hops.
[03:44] Priya Nair: quantization — have customers lost quality moving to 4-bit? how does that affect throughput?
[03:49] Diego Ramos: quantization tradeoffs: INT8/4-bit can drop memory bandwidth and increase throughput dramatically, esp on batch decode. On many open models we see 1.8-2.5x throughput improvements moving from FP16 to 4-bit with small quality regressions; depends on model and eval set. we recommend A/B evals on your prompts.
[04:07] Samir Patel: can quantized models run on the same runtime alongside FP16? how do rollouts work?
[04:12] Alyssa Chen: yes — runtime can host multiple model variants and route requests. rollouts can be done with canary percentages; you can route a small % to a quantized variant and compare quality metrics via eval hooks.
[04:23] Priya Nair: ok great. can we talk specifics — max_num_seqs values and expected throughput numbers?
[04:28] Diego Ramos: sure — rough numbers from our p4d bench with a 7B-ish model: max_num_seqs=16 and batch_timeout_ms=10 gives you low-latency tail (~120ms 95th) at moderate throughput. bump to max_num_seqs=48 and batch_timeout_ms=25 you can often double throughput but 95th goes up ~60-80ms. max_batch_tokens affects packing for mixed seq lengths — a high max_batch_tokens like 8192 allows denser packing.
[04:54] Ben Turner: are those per-worker or cluster-wide knobs? where do we tune them?
[04:58] Diego Ramos: per-route and per-deployment. You can set defaults globally and override per-model or per-route. The scheduler reads route hints at request time. For your use case we likely set aggressive knobs on the high-volume route and conservative knobs on low-latency admin routes.
[05:12] Priya Nair: how do you prevent head-of-line blocking when a large seq hits the queue?
[05:16] Diego Ramos: heuristics: if a sequence exceeds a token threshold (e.g., > 512 tokens), we either dispatch it immediately (single-seq batch) or place it in a separate long-seq queue. Also we do dynamic packing to avoid wasting slots on small seqs.
[05:30] Samir Patel: any concerns about GPU memory when increasing batch sizes with quantized models?
[05:34] Diego Ramos: quantization reduces memory, but larger batch sizes increase ephemeral activation memory. we have memory-safe packers that compute worst-case activation and will cap batch sizes to avoid OOMs. that's where max_batch_tokens is critical.
[05:46] Alyssa Chen: let's walk through a sample tuning plan for Nimbus. Diego?
[05:49] Diego Ramos: plan: 1) collect representative request traces (Ben), including token-length histograms and percentiles, arrival distributions. 2) run knob sweep on a staging p4d replica: vary max_num_seqs [8,16,32,48,64], batch_timeout_ms [5,10,20,30], max_batch_tokens [2048,4096,8192], and quantization variants (FP16, 8-bit, 4-bit). 3) capture throughput (seqs/s), GPU utilization, latency pctls, and cache hit rates. 4) pick tradeoff point and run 2-hour pilot.
[06:18] Priya Nair: what metrics should we collect exactly?
[06:21] Diego Ramos: request latency pctls (50/90/95/99), GPU utilization, tokens/s, effective cost / token, KV cache hit rates, batch size distribution, and per-worker queue lengths. Also trace a few requests to see decode vs encode split.
[06:34] Ben Turner: do you provide tooling to collect these automatically?
[06:37] Diego Ramos: yes — Redwood Console exposes route dashboards and per-worker traces. For pilots we'll give you a CSV exporter and an example Prometheus scrape.
[06:45] Priya Nair: about the cache — is it shared across workers or per-worker?
[06:49] Diego Ramos: KV cache is per-replica to avoid cross-network serialization; however, we do prefix-aware routing so requests from the same user/session tend to hit the same replica when sticky routing is enabled. for private deployments you can opt for a shared cache service but that adds complexity.
[07:05] Samir Patel: sticky routing — does that create hot-shards if one session is very active?
[07:09] Diego Ramos: it can. we mitigate with consistent-hashing + rebalancing and session eviction policies. the scheduler also supports spillover to other replicas if a shard exceeds a threshold.
[07:21] Alyssa Chen: question from sales side — do we need to talk about pricing implications of dedicated pilot?
[07:25] Samir Patel: yes, we care. but let's get the tech right first.
[07:28] Diego Ramos: benchmark numbers: on p4d with FP16, baseline 7B model 100 tokens average, you might get ~1.6k seqs/s per GPU with moderate knobs. With 4-bit quant, same config can push ~3k seqs/s. these are rough — depends on decoding length and beam settings.
[07:47] Priya Nair: that's promising. our 95th <200ms requirement — is that realistic with 3k sps?
[07:52] Diego Ramos: with continuous batching and optimized knobs it's plausible if your average tokens are moderate and you split heavy-long requests into a separate queue. The pilot will validate.
[07:59] Ben Turner: any recommended default starting knobs for us to test?
[08:02] Diego Ramos: start with max_num_seqs=32, batch_timeout_ms=15, max_batch_tokens=4096, quant=FP16. Then run sweeps increasing seqs to 48/64 and explore 4-bit on the best config.
[08:16] Priya Nair: what about function/tool calling and streaming — do they impact batching?
[08:20] Diego Ramos: yes streaming reduces the ability to pack tokens because you emit partial tokens; function-calls usually finish sooner and are smaller payloads, but streaming responses can bypass some batching. We treat streaming as a separate path with tighter timeouts.
[08:34] Samir Patel: can we test with our actual eval prompts? we have 5000 benchmark prompts.
[08:38] Alyssa Chen: absolutely — Ben will share a sampled set and Diego will run them as part of the knob sweep. we'll need to anonymize any PII.
[08:47] Ben Turner: noted, will sanitize and upload.
[08:50] Priya Nair: latency vs cost question — if we add more replications to reduce tail, cost increases. what's Redwood's approach to balancing this?
[08:58] Diego Ramos: we offer autoscaling and prioritized routing. For example, keep a small hot pool for low-latency routes (higher cost), and a pooled cold cluster for throughput. Also caching reduces effective tokens and thus cost. We'll show a cost/latency curve for your traces.
[09:12] Samir Patel: security and VPC checklist — Priya wants those docs.
[09:16] Alyssa Chen: yes I'll send SOC2 and VPC config docs after this call.
[09:20] Priya Nair: thanks. any gotchas on on-prem GPUs?
[09:23] Diego Ramos: driver mismatches and NCCL versions are common issues. also different interconnect (InfiniBand) needs tuning. Our private deployment team has a checklist.
[09:33] Ben Turner: about node-level scheduling — can we pin certain routes to GPUs with different quantization variants?
[09:37] Diego Ramos: yes, node affinity is supported. You can tag a model variant and pin to nodes with quant-optimized drivers.
[09:44] Alyssa Chen: ok, let's recap next steps. Diego, can you summarize pilot plan and knobs to sweep?
[09:50] Diego Ramos: sure — (1) Ben provides request traces & token histograms; (2) Diego runs knob sweep across max_num_seqs [8,16,32,48,64], batch_timeout_ms [5,10,15,25,40], max_batch_tokens [2048,4096,8192], quant variants FP16/8/4-bit; (3) collect latency pctls, throughput, GPU util, KV hit rate; (4) run 2-hr dedicated pilot on p4d at chosen config; (5) validate 95th latency and cost per token.
[10:22] Priya Nair: timeline?
[10:24] Alyssa Chen: we'll aim to have the sweep results and config spreadsheet by 2025-09-25 and pilot onboarding in the following week.
[10:30] Samir Patel: sounds good.
[10:33] Ben Turner: one last question — do you support mixed-precision within a single model deploy? like FP16 for attention and 4-bit quant for FFN?
[10:40] Diego Ramos: mixed-precision kernels are an area of active work. some architectures support mixed quant/per-layer; currently we support per-variant quantization (whole model), but we have experimental mixed kernels for certain layers. We can include that in the engineering notes.
[10:54] Alyssa Chen: perfect. we'll send the checklist and spreadsheet. thanks everyone.
[10:58] Priya Nair: thanks, very helpful.
[11:00] Samir Patel: thanks all.
[11:02] (end)
